Aggregation and cross-level workflows

Source: vignettes/cross-level-workflows.Rmd
cross-level-workflows.Rmd
library(priogridR)

Cross-level analysis is not a single neutral operation. A population total may be divided between overlapping regions, whereas a rate should normally be averaged using the area represented by each source observation. The functions in this vignette require that distinction to be stated explicitly.

Grouped summaries

pg_aggregate() provides ordinary grouped summaries without introducing a package-specific data class.

cells <- data.frame(
  region = c("a", "a", "b"),
  events = c(1, 2, 4),
  population = c(100, 200, 150)
)

pg_aggregate(
  cells,
  values = c("events", "population"),
  by = "region",
  fun = "sum"
)
#>   region events population
#> 1      a      3        300
#> 2      b      4        150

Weights may be supplied for means. Weighted totals are handled separately by pg_area_weight() because they require a substantive allocation rule.

Construct a spatial crosswalk

The target polygons are supplied by the researcher. This makes the source, date, and territorial definition of administrative or country boundaries part of the reproducible workflow.

config <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 18, ncol = 36, verbose = FALSE)

regions <- pg_geometry(342:344, config = config)
regions$region_id <- c("a", "a", "b")

crosswalk <- pg_crosswalk(
  regions,
  target_id = "region_id",
  pgid = 342:344,
  assignment = "fractional",
  config = config
)

crosswalk
#>   pgid region_id overlap_area_km2 allocation_area_km2 cell_fraction
#> 1  342         a          1233205             1233205             1
#> 2  343         a          1233205             1233205             1
#> 3  344         b          1233205             1233205             1
#>   target_fraction
#> 1             0.5
#> 2             0.5
#> 3             1.0

Repeated target identifiers are dissolved before intersection. Fractional assignment returns every positive-area overlap. assignment = "largest" assigns the whole source cell to the target with its largest overlap, while assignment = "centroid" uses the cell centre. Overlapping targets make a centroid assignment ambiguous and therefore produce an error.

The returned diagnostics distinguish:

  • overlap_area_km2: the observed geometric intersection;
  • allocation_area_km2: the area used to weight intensive values;
  • cell_fraction: the share of an extensive cell total assigned to a target;
  • target_fraction: the share of the target represented by the intersection.

Extensive and intensive variables

An extensive variable is additive over space. Population counts and event counts are common examples. An intensive variable describes a local level or rate and should not normally be summed.

grid_data <- data.frame(
  pgid = 342:344,
  population = c(100, 200, 300),
  rate = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.4)
)

transferred <- pg_area_weight(
  grid_data,
  crosswalk,
  values = c("population", "rate"),
  target_id = "region_id",
  variable_type = c(
    population = "extensive",
    rate = "intensive"
  )
)

transferred
#>   region_id population population_coverage rate rate_coverage
#> 1         a        300                   1 0.15             1
#> 2         b        300                   1 0.40             1

Each output variable receives a _coverage column. It is the share of the relevant allocation weight represented by non-missing values. With na_rm = FALSE, incomplete coverage produces a missing estimate but the coverage diagnostic remains available.

Aggregate to countries

pg_to_country() combines crosswalk construction and value transfer. It does not download or bundle a particular country-boundary dataset.

country_result <- pg_to_country(
  grid_data,
  countries = regions,
  country_id = "region_id",
  values = "population",
  variable_type = "extensive",
  return_crosswalk = TRUE,
  config = config
)

country_result$data
#>   region_id population population_coverage
#> 1         a        300                   1
#> 2         b        300                   1

Setting return_crosswalk = TRUE makes the exact spatial allocation available for inspection, storage, and reuse.

One boundary definition is used in each call. When a historical panel spans territorial changes, split it into documented boundary vintages, call pg_to_country() separately for each vintage, and then combine the results. This prevents the package from silently applying present-day borders to past observations.

Change grid resolution

Resolution changes use the same extensive-versus-intensive rules.

fine <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 18, ncol = 36, verbose = FALSE)
coarse <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 9, ncol = 18, verbose = FALSE)
fine_ids <- c(342L, 343L, 378L, 379L)
coordinates <- pg_coords_from_id(fine_ids, config = fine)

fine_data <- data.frame(
  pgid = fine_ids,
  population = rep(10, 4),
  rate = ifelse(coordinates$xcoord < 0, 2, 4)
)

coarse_data <- pg_change_resolution(
  fine_data,
  values = c("population", "rate"),
  from_config = fine,
  to_config = coarse,
  variable_type = c(
    population = "extensive",
    rate = "intensive"
  )
)

coarse_data
#>   pgid population population_coverage rate rate_coverage
#> 1   81  10.077138                   1    2             1
#> 2   82  10.077138                   1    4             1
#> 3   99   9.922862                   1    2             1
#> 4  100   9.922862                   1    4             1

Extensive totals are fractionally allocated, so a complete transformation preserves their global sum apart from numerical tolerance. Intensive values are averaged with allocated area as the weight.

Compare alternative representations

After two alternatives have been placed on the same grid, pg_compare_resolutions() can return either row-level differences or compact diagnostics.

alternative <- coarse_data
alternative$rate <- alternative$rate + c(0.1, -0.1)

pg_compare_resolutions(
  coarse_data,
  alternative,
  values = c("population", "rate")
)
#>     variable n_reference n_candidate n_matched reference_coverage
#> 1 population           4           4         4                  1
#> 2       rate           4           4         4                  1
#>   candidate_coverage mean_difference mean_absolute_difference rmse correlation
#> 1                  1               0                      0.0  0.0           1
#> 2                  1               0                      0.1  0.1           1

pg_compare_resolutions(
  coarse_data,
  alternative,
  values = "rate",
  detail = "cells"
)
#>   pgid rate_reference rate_candidate rate_difference rate_absolute_difference
#> 1   81              2            2.1             0.1                      0.1
#> 2   82              4            3.9            -0.1                      0.1
#> 3   99              2            2.1             0.1                      0.1
#> 4  100              4            3.9            -0.1                      0.1
#>   rate_relative_difference
#> 1                    0.050
#> 2                   -0.025
#> 3                    0.050
#> 4                   -0.025

The summary reports matching coverage, mean difference, mean absolute difference, root mean squared error, and correlation. These diagnostics do not decide which spatial representation is substantively preferable; they expose the consequences of that choice.
